title: Keys and relationships
objective: Identify primary keys, foreign keys and the grain of each table, predict how many rows a join returns, and use joins to verify relationships (children per parent, orphan keys).
context: Before the analytics team trusts any joined report, the data-quality lead wants proof that the relationships in the warehouse hold: does every order point at a real customer? every product at a real supplier? how many lines does an order have? Joins are only as correct as your understanding of the keys underneath them.

exercises.title: Look up the order behind each return
exercises.question: Customer care wants each return shown next to the order and product it came from.
exercises.prompt: Return one row per return with columns return_id, order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity and refund_amount (order_id, product_id and quantity come from order_items).
hints: returns.order_item_id is a foreign key to order_items' primary key.
Driving table = returns (one row per return). Every return should find exactly one line.
FROM returns AS r JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_item_id = r.order_item_id
exercises.why: Looking up parent attributes from a child row is the most common join there is. Because you join to the parent's primary key, the row count cannot grow.

recall.q: Joining a child table to its parent's primary key: can the row count grow?
recall.a: No. Each child row matches at most one parent row, so the count stays the same (or shrinks with INNER if the FK is orphaned).

exercises.join_notes: returns has 10 rows, order_items 150. The key order_item_id is the PRIMARY key of order_items, so each return matches exactly one line: 10 in → 10 out, no multiplication. No return points at a missing line, so INNER JOIN drops nothing and no NULLs appear. The other 140 order lines were never returned — they simply have no partner in returns, which is fine because the question is about returns.

exercises.title: Orders per customer (children per parent)
exercises.question: Sales wants to know how many orders each customer has placed (any status).
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name and order_count (number of orders of any status) for every customer who has at least one order.
hints: One customer → many orders. Join, then GROUP BY the parent's key.
Group by customer_id (not by name — customers 3 and 4 are both 'John Smith').
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON ... GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;
exercises.why: 'Count children per parent' is how you profile a relationship: who has many, who has few, who has none.

recall.q: Why group by customer_id rather than name?
recall.a: Names are not keys — two different customers (3 and 4) are both 'John Smith'; grouping by name would merge them.

exercises.join_notes: customers has 20 rows, orders 60. Before GROUP BY, the join produces 59 rows: each order repeats its customer's columns (customer 1 appears 9 times — one-to-many multiplication). One order is lost: order 31 points at customer 99, who does not exist, so INNER JOIN silently drops it. After GROUP BY we get 17 customers; customers 18, 19 and 20 have no orders and vanish from an INNER JOIN (Lesson 11 brings them back with LEFT JOIN). The 17 order_counts add up to 59, not 60.

exercises.title: Grain check: what does the join do to row counts?
exercises.question: The data-quality lead wants a one-row reconciliation of orders vs. order lines.
exercises.prompt: Return a single row with columns orders_rows (rows in orders), order_items_rows (rows in order_items), joined_rows (rows produced by INNER JOINing orders to order_items on order_id) and orders_in_join (number of DISTINCT order_ids in that join).
hints: A scalar subquery like (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) can sit in the SELECT list.
COUNT(*) counts joined rows; COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) counts orders that survived.

SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) AS orders_rows, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items) AS order_items_rows, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders_in_join FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON ...
exercises.why: Comparing input and output row counts is the single best habit for catching join bugs: it tells you instantly whether a join multiplied or dropped rows.

recall.q: After joining orders (parent) to order_items (child), what is the grain of the result?
recall.a: One row per order line — the grain of the 'many' side.

exercises.join_notes: orders_rows = 60, order_items_rows = 150, joined_rows = 150, orders_in_join = 59. The join has the grain of order_items: every line finds its order, so 150 lines → 150 rows (orders with 5 lines appear 5 times). Only 59 distinct orders survive: order 60 (pending) has no lines, so INNER JOIN drops it. No NULLs appear in an INNER JOIN.

exercises.title: Find orphan orders
exercises.question: Finance found revenue that cannot be attributed to any customer. Which orders point at a customer that does not exist?
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, customer_id and order_date for every order whose customer_id has no matching row in customers.
hints: You need to keep orders that find NO customer — an INNER JOIN would throw exactly those away.
LEFT JOIN customers, then keep rows where the customer side came back NULL.
FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL
exercises.why: Orphan foreign keys are a classic data-quality defect (late-arriving dimensions, deleted customers, test data). Every INNER JOIN on that key silently loses these rows — and their revenue.

recall.a: LEFT JOIN the other table and keep only rows WHERE right_table.key IS NULL (or use NOT EXISTS).

exercises.join_notes: orders has 60 rows; the LEFT JOIN keeps all 60 (each order matches 0 or 1 customer, so no multiplication). 59 find their customer; order 31 (customer_id 99) finds none, so every customers column is NULL on that row. The WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL keeps exactly that one row. Note: we test the RIGHT table's key — o.customer_id is 99, not NULL.

exercises.title: Broken vs. missing supplier keys
exercises.question: Procurement asks: which products reference a supplier_id that does not exist in the supplier table?
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name and supplier_id for products whose supplier_id is NOT NULL but has no matching supplier. (Products with a NULL supplier_id are a different problem — exclude them.)
hints: Same anti-join pattern as the orphan-orders exercise, on products → suppliers.
A NULL FK also fails to match; separate it with p.supplier_id IS NOT NULL.
FROM products p LEFT JOIN suppliers s ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id WHERE p.supplier_id IS NOT NULL AND s.supplier_id IS NULL
exercises.why: 'Broken key' (points nowhere) and 'missing key' (NULL) need different fixes: one is a bad reference to repair, the other is unassigned data to fill in. Report them separately.

recall.q: Does NULL = NULL match in a join condition?
recall.a: No. NULL = NULL is NULL (unknown), so rows with a NULL key never match anything.

exercises.join_notes: products has 25 rows, suppliers 5. The LEFT JOIN returns 25 rows (each product matches at most one supplier). 23 match; two come back with NULL supplier columns: product 21 (supplier_id 9 — no such supplier, a broken key) and product 22 (supplier_id NULL — a missing key; NULL never equals anything). The extra filter p.supplier_id IS NOT NULL removes product 22, leaving 1 row: product 21.

exercises.title: Products per supplier, including zero
exercises.question: Procurement wants the size of each supplier's catalogue — including suppliers we list but buy nothing from.
exercises.prompt: Return supplier_id, supplier_name and product_count (number of products referencing that supplier; 0 when none) for all 5 suppliers.
hints: 'All 5 suppliers' means suppliers must survive even without products.
COUNT(*) would count the NULL-padded row as 1; count a right-table column instead.
FROM suppliers s LEFT JOIN products p ON p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id ... COUNT(p.product_id) AS product_count
exercises.why: Zero is a real answer. A parent with no children is often the most interesting row (an unused supplier contract, a customer who never bought).

recall.q: After a LEFT JOIN, why COUNT(p.product_id) instead of COUNT(*)?
recall.a: COUNT(*) counts the NULL-padded row of an unmatched parent as 1; COUNT(column) skips NULLs and correctly gives 0.

exercises.join_notes: suppliers 5 rows, products 25. Before grouping the LEFT JOIN yields 24 rows: 23 products that match a supplier (one-to-many: suppliers 1, 2 and 3 repeat 6 times, supplier 4 five times) plus 1 NULL-padded row for supplier 5 (Andes Trading), which has no products. COUNT(p.product_id) turns that NULL row into 0. Products 21 (supplier 9) and 22 (NULL supplier) never appear — they belong to no listed supplier, so the counts add to 23, not 25.

worked_example.question: How many rows do orders and order_items have, and how many rows does joining them produce?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders)      AS orders_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items) AS order_items_rows,
       COUNT(*)                           AS joined_rows
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id;
worked_example.explanation: 60 orders × (1 to 5 lines each) → 150 joined rows: exactly the number of order lines, because each line has exactly one order (many-to-one) and order 60 (pending, no lines) has nothing to pair with. The joined result has the grain of the *many* side — one row per order line.

recipe:
**Keys in this warehouse**

| table | primary key (one row per…) | foreign keys (points to…) |
|---|---|---|
| customers | customer_id (customer) | — |
| suppliers | supplier_id (supplier) | — |
| products | product_id (product) | supplier_id → suppliers |
| orders | order_id (order) | customer_id → customers |
| order_items | order_item_id (order line) | order_id → orders, product_id → products |
| returns | return_id (return) | order_item_id → order_items |

- **Primary key (PK):** unique, never NULL — defines the table's **grain** ("one row per ___").
- **Foreign key (FK):** a column that *should* match a PK elsewhere. SQLite here does **not** enforce it,
  so orphans exist (order 31 → customer 99, product 21 → supplier 9) — and NULL FKs (product 22).
- **One-to-many:** one customer → many orders; one order → many lines. Joining parent to child produces
  **one row per child**: the parent's columns repeat. The result's grain is the *many* side.
- **Many-to-one lookup:** joining child → parent (lines → products) keeps the child count (if every FK matches).

**The join recipe — do it in this order, every time, before typing SQL**

1. **Pick the driving table.** Which table's rows is the answer *about*? ("every customer…", "each order line…")
   That table goes first, after `FROM` — it is the **left table**.
2. **Name the right table(s) and the shared key.** What column links them? Is it PK → FK (one-to-many) or
   one-to-one? Which side is the "many" side?
3. **Ask: "must every row of the left table survive, even with no match?"**
   - no → `INNER JOIN` (unmatched rows silently disappear)
   - yes → `LEFT JOIN` (unmatched rows stay, right-side columns become NULL)
   - rows from *both* sides must survive → `FULL OUTER JOIN`
4. **Predict the row count before you run it.** Count the inputs (`SELECT COUNT(*) …`), think about
   matches per row (0, 1 or many), write your guess down — then run and compare. A surprise means
   you misunderstood the grain, the key or the data.

```sql
-- children per parent: grain = parent after GROUP BY
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM   customers AS c                         -- driving (left) table
JOIN   orders    AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id   -- shared key
GROUP  BY c.customer_id, c.name;

-- orphan check: child rows whose FK finds no parent
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id
FROM   orders AS o
LEFT JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE  c.customer_id IS NULL;
```
common_mistakes: Assuming a foreign key is enforced. In most warehouses (Snowflake included) FK constraints are informational only — orphans happen.
Not knowing the grain of a table before joining it, then being surprised when parent columns repeat.
Grouping by a name instead of the key (two 'John Smith' customers merge into one).
Testing the LEFT table's column for NULL in an anti-join; you must test the RIGHT table's key.
Using COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN, which turns 'no children' into 1.
recall: What defines the grain of a table?
Its primary key — 'one row per <PK>'. E.g. order_items: one row per order line.
Joining a parent (1) to a child (many): what is the result's row count?
The number of matching child rows — parent columns repeat once per child.
Name two ways a foreign key can fail to match.
It points to a non-existent key (orphan, e.g. customer 99) or it is NULL (e.g. product 22's supplier).
What do you do before running any join?
Predict the row count from the input counts and the key relationship.
review_next: Lesson 10 formalises INNER JOIN. Keep the numbers from this lesson in mind: 60 orders, 150 lines, 20 customers, 25 products, 5 suppliers — you will predict join sizes from them constantly.
